opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to where the leverage is. If you look at what's happened over the last few years, the model architectures have largely converged. Everyone's more or less using some variant of the transformer, and the training recipes, whether it's pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, or the various flavors of RL, are increasingly well understood and openly available. The compute side is getting commoditized too; you can rent GPUs, and there are great open-source frameworks for training. So when you ask, what actually differentiates one model from another, the answer more and more is the data.

And that was something I saw firsthand before starting this. When you're working on models at scale, a huge fraction of the effort, and frankly most of the gains, came from getting the data right. Deciding what goes in, filtering out what's noisy or redundant, generating synthetic data to fill gaps, balancing the mixture. These things moved the needle far more than tweaking a learning rate or adding a layer.

But the problem is that this work is still incredibly manual and ad hoc for most teams. People write one-off scripts, they eyeball samples, they iterate slowly. It's not systematized the way model training has become. So if you're an enterprise or a startup that wants a custom model, say a smaller model that's really good at your specific task, the bottleneck usually isn't, can I fine-tune? It's, do I have the right data to fine-tune on? Often you don't have enough, or it's not in the right format, or the quality is uneven.

Synthetic data has also changed the picture a lot. With strong frontier models, you can now generate, refine, and filter data at a scale that wasn't possible before. That opens up a real opportunity: if you can build good tooling around curation, generation, and evaluation, you can help people go from a vague idea of what they want their model to do to a high-quality dataset that actually gets them there. So to me, data curation felt like the highest-leverage problem, and also one that's underserved relative to how much it matters.

r001.rationale: It says that for custom models, the usual bottleneck is having the right fine-tuning data, which is often insufficient, incorrectly formatted, or uneven in quality.

r002.rationale: It compares where effort and gains lie across models, training, compute, and data, then identifies curation as the highest-leverage problem to focus on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we started Bespoke Labs, the question we kept asking ourselves was: if you're a team that wants a model that's really good at your specific task, what's actually hard about that? And the honest answer is, it's not the training. Fine-tuning has gotten pretty commoditized. There are great open-source recipes, there are platforms that will run the training for you, the infrastructure is mostly solved. If you have good data, getting a strong model out the other end is almost mechanical at this point.

What's not solved is getting that data. And I'd seen this firsthand at Google, where I worked on recommendation systems and later on some of the large model efforts. Almost all the real gains came from being smarter about what you fed the model, not from the architecture. Everyone's working with roughly the same transformers. The differentiator is the data.

And the way people build datasets today is still really ad hoc. It's a bunch of notebooks, a bunch of scripts calling an LLM to generate examples, someone eyeballs a few rows and says it looks fine, and then you train and hope. There's no good tooling for it, there's not much reproducibility, and critically there's not much of a feedback loop. You don't know which examples actually helped, which hurt, where the gaps in coverage are.

So we think of data curation really broadly. It's synthetic generation, yes, but it's also filtering, deduplication, verification, deciding what the right distribution of difficulty is, figuring out how to rejection-sample reasoning traces so you only keep the ones that are correct. When we did the Bespoke-Stratos work, distilling reasoning from DeepSeek R1, the thing that made it work with a relatively small number of examples was that curation step. Which prompts, which answers we kept, how we checked correctness. That's where the leverage was.

The other reason I think it's the right place to focus is that it compounds. If you build the pipeline well, you can regenerate, iterate, scale it up when a better teacher model comes out. If you've just built a model, you've got a static artifact. We want people to be able to own the process, not just the weights. That's kind of why we built Curator the way we did, as an open-source library where you can express those pipelines explicitly and see what's happening.

r001.rationale: The response says fine-tuning is largely solved, while obtaining and curating good data remains unsolved; it describes dataset creation as ad hoc and training as a matter of hoping for the best.

r002.rationale: It describes asking what is actually hard in building a task-specific model, identifying data as the bottleneck, and focusing effort there because that is where the gains come from.

astra-6.text:
When you’re building a custom model, what makes it custom is really your data—the examples that capture the task you care about. You can start with a very capable pretrained model, but you still have to decide what to teach it. And that’s where a lot of the difficult work is.

You might have a large amount of data, but how much of it is relevant? How much is duplicated? Are there errors in the labels? Are you covering the cases your model will actually encounter? Simply adding more data doesn’t necessarily solve those problems.

So I see curation as a way to make that process more deliberate. You look at where the model is failing, understand what’s missing from the dataset, and select or collect examples that address those gaps. That gives people a practical way to improve a model for their particular use case.

r001.rationale: The response calls data curation difficult and useful, but does not say that fine-tuning projects commonly fail at this stage.

r002.rationale: It describes finding dataset gaps to improve a model, but does not present identifying a complex problem’s critical bottleneck as a way to choose where to focus problem-solving.

sol-6.1.text:
When you’re building a custom model, you’re trying to get it to do well on something specific to your business. And a lot of what determines whether it succeeds is the data you give it. Does that data represent the cases you care about? Are there gaps? Are you repeatedly showing it essentially the same examples?

You can have a very large dataset and still be missing the examples that would actually help the model improve. So the challenge is figuring out what to keep, what to label, and what additional data to collect. That’s why I see data curation as such a useful place to focus: it gives people a way to improve their models by making better decisions about what those models learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says data curation is a useful focus for custom models, but does not say fine-tuning projects commonly fail at that stage.

r002.rationale: It explains why data curation matters, but does not present identifying a complex problem’s critical bottleneck as a general way to choose where to focus.
